facts.text: Moundville Archaeological Park, a National Historic Landmark, preserves 26 Mississippian earthwork mounds that once hosted a thriving ceremonial center.
The park sits on the Black Warrior River, where visitors can walk among 29 earthen mounds that date back nearly a millennium.
National Geographic dubbed Moundville the “Big Apple of the 14th Century,” noting it was once America’s largest city north of Mexico.
Moundville’s historic roots stretch back to the Mississippian culture, making it a key site for understanding prehistoric Native American life in the Southeast.
The town’s name honors the ancient mounds that dominate the landscape, a reminder of the region’s deep archaeological heritage.
In the 1930s, photographer Walker Evans and writer James Agee captured everyday life in Moundville, later publishing their work in Let Us Now Praise Famous Men.
